subject: Polity
topic: Union Executive — Vice President and PM
sub_topic: Council of Ministers — composition and responsibility

concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Council of Ministers: Articles 74 and 75
key_dimensions: Article 74(1): mandatory nature of ministerial aid and advice — 'shall be' vs. original discretionary language pre-44th Amendment
Article 75: appointment, tenure, salaries, and oath of ministers
The President's power to require reconsideration of advice (Article 74(1) proviso) — one-time binding reconsideration trap
Judicial non-justiciability of ministerial advice under Article 74(2) — UPSC trap on what courts cannot inquire into

concepts.name: Three-Tier Ministerial Hierarchy: Cabinet, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers
key_dimensions: Constitutional silence on 'Cabinet' — the term 'Cabinet' appears only in Article 352, not in Article 74/75
Distinction between 'Council of Ministers' (Article 74) and 'Cabinet' — constitutional vs. political executive trap
Ministers of State: independent charge vs. attached to Cabinet Minister — functional difference
Deputy Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries: constitutional vs. statutory/conventional basis

concepts.name: Cabinet: Legal Status, Composition, and Dominant Position
key_dimensions: Cabinet defined only in Article 352(3) — inserted by 44th Amendment Act 1978
Cabinet as the 'inner ring' of Council of Ministers — not a constitutionally mandated separate body for routine governance
Role of Cabinet in proclamation of National Emergency: written communication requirement
Cabinet committees — constitutional basis absent, yet critical to governance (trap: are they constitutional bodies?)

concepts.name: Appointment of Prime Minister and Council of Ministers: Procedure and Conventions
key_dimensions: Article 75(1): Ministers appointed by President 'on the advice of PM' — President has no discretion except in hung Parliament
Constitutional convention vs. constitutional law in PM appointment — role of floor test
President's discretion in appointing PM when no clear majority: Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission recommendations
Can a non-member of Parliament be appointed as PM/Minister? — Article 75(5): six-month window trap

concepts.name: Eligibility and Disqualification of Ministers: Article 75(5) and Related Provisions
key_dimensions: Minister must be a member of either House within six months of appointment — Article 75(5)
Which House must a minister belong to? — No constitutional compulsion to be from Lok Sabha (even PM can be from Rajya Sabha)
Disqualification under Tenth Schedule: does it affect ministerial post? — Anti-defection and ministerial office interplay
Disqualification under Articles 102 and 191: office of profit trap as applied to ministers

concepts.name: Collective Responsibility of Council of Ministers: Article 75(3)
key_dimensions: Article 75(3): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha — NOT to Rajya Sabha (critical UPSC trap)
Meaning of collective responsibility: Cabinet decisions binding on all ministers, including dissenters
Confidence motion vs. no-confidence motion — procedural difference and constitutional implications
Does collective responsibility extend to Ministers of State? — Constitutional vs. conventional answer

concepts.name: Individual Responsibility of Ministers: Convention and Constitutional Interplay
key_dimensions: No explicit constitutional provision for individual ministerial responsibility — purely conventional
PM's power to ask a minister to resign vs. advising President to dismiss: Article 75(2) trap
Relationship between individual and collective responsibility — minister who disagrees must resign or stay silent
Accountability to Parliament through Question Hour, motions, committees — tools of individual accountability

concepts.name: Tenure of Ministers: Pleasure Doctrine under Article 75(2)
key_dimensions: Article 75(2): Ministers hold office during 'pleasure of President' — but this pleasure is exercised only on PM's advice
Can President dismiss a minister independently? — Constitutional answer vs. political reality
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974): President/Governor must act on ministerial advice — judicial affirmation
Vacancy in PM's office: entire Council of Ministers deemed to have vacated — constitutional automaticity

concepts.name: Vote of No-Confidence and Its Constitutional Mechanics
key_dimensions: No-confidence motion in Lok Sabha only — Rajya Sabha cannot pass it (Article 75(3) trap)
Effect of no-confidence: entire Council falls, not just PM — collective responsibility consequence
Rules of Procedure: 50-member support requirement to introduce no-confidence motion
Distinction from censure motion, cut motion, and adjournment motion — UPSC frequently tests these overlaps

concepts.name: Size of Council of Ministers: 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003
key_dimensions: Article 75(1A): total ministers (including PM) not to exceed 15% of total strength of Lok Sabha
Minimum floor: not less than 12 ministers even if 15% yields a lower number — trap on minimum vs. maximum
Same cap applies to states under Article 164(1A) — federal symmetry
Anti-defection linkage: disqualified members cannot be ministers — Article 75(1B) and 164(1B)

concepts.name: Oath of Ministers: Form and Implications under Article 75(4)
key_dimensions: Third Schedule: two oaths — oath of office and oath of secrecy — both administered by President
Oath of secrecy: basis for collective responsibility and Cabinet confidentiality
Can oath be administered before Parliament membership? — Yes, with six-month window (Article 75(5))
Violation of oath: not a directly enforceable legal remedy but has political and moral consequences

concepts.name: Prime Minister's Special Constitutional Position and Powers
key_dimensions: PM as 'keystone of the Cabinet arch' — Morley's phrase frequently quoted in UPSC context
Article 78: PM's duties to President — communication of Cabinet decisions, furnishing information
PM's role in summoning and proroguing Parliament (Article 85) — advice-based exercise
PM chairs Cabinet meetings, allocates portfolios, and can recommend dissolution of Lok Sabha — all conventional, not constitutional

concepts.name: Prime Minister and President: Relationship, Tensions, and Constitutional Boundaries
key_dimensions: Article 74(1) post-44th Amendment: advice is binding; President can send back once for reconsideration
President's 'pocket veto' on ministerial advice — practical possibility vs. constitutional intent
Instances of constitutional friction: 1979 Charan Singh government, 1997 Gujral episode
44th Amendment significance: changed 'may' to 'shall' in Article 74 — making advice binding

concepts.name: Cabinet Committees: Types, Functions, and Constitutional Status
key_dimensions: Cabinet committees are extra-constitutional — created by executive order, not by Constitution
Standing vs. ad hoc committees — examples: Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS), Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA)
PM chairs most Cabinet committees — reinforces PM's dominant position
Decisions of Cabinet committees are equivalent to Cabinet decisions — though not constitutionally mandated

concepts.name: Parliamentary Accountability Mechanisms for Council of Ministers
key_dimensions: Question Hour, Zero Hour, and Half-an-Hour Discussion — tools targeting individual ministers
No-confidence motion and confidence motion — tools targeting collective responsibility
Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs): examine demands for grants, bills — ministry-wise scrutiny
Annual reports, CAG reports tabled in Parliament — accountability without direct vote mechanism

concepts.name: Distinction Between De Jure and De Facto Executive: President vs. PM/Cabinet
key_dimensions: Constitutional design: President as de jure executive; PM and Cabinet as de facto executive
All executive power vested in President (Article 53) but exercised on Cabinet advice — the core constitutional paradox
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006): President's satisfaction must be based on Cabinet advice, not personal view
British model comparison: 'King reigns but does not govern' — India's adaptation and where it differs

concepts.name: Role of Council of Ministers in Constitutional Emergency Provisions
key_dimensions: National Emergency (Article 352): Cabinet's written recommendation is a mandatory precondition — 44th Amendment safeguard
President's Rule (Article 356): Council of Ministers advises, but Governor's report is the trigger — chain of advice
Financial Emergency (Article 360): Cabinet advice required — President cannot act suo motu
Revocation of emergencies: Parliament's role vs. Cabinet's role — who can revoke and under what conditions

concepts.name: Allocation and Change of Portfolios: Constitutional and Conventional Framework
key_dimensions: No constitutional provision specifying portfolio allocation — entirely at PM's discretion advised to President
Independent charge ministries vs. attached ministries — administrative significance
Reshuffle conventions: PM can reshuffle without fresh election mandate — no constitutional bar
Multi-portfolio ministers: constitutional permissibility vs. administrative efficiency debate

concepts.name: Caretaker Government: Constitutional Status and Limitations
key_dimensions: No explicit constitutional mention of 'caretaker government' — purely conventional status
Triggered when Lok Sabha is dissolved or no-confidence is passed — Council continues till new government
Limitations: caretaker government should avoid major policy decisions — convention, not law
Election Commission guidelines during Model Code of Conduct — practical constraints on caretaker Council

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law and Its Impact on Ministerial Accountability
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985): disqualification for voting against party whip
Article 75(1B): a disqualified member cannot be appointed as minister — direct constitutional bar
Conflict between collective Cabinet responsibility and party whip discipline in Parliament
Speaker's role in disqualification vs. ministerial status — judicial review permissibility post-Kihoto Hollohan (1992)
